/packages/backend/src/i18n/locales/en.js: These server messages appear across the web app: mostly errors and status notices for accounts, transactions, budgets, bank connections, investments, loans, imports and AI settings, plus tag reminder titles in the notifications list. Signed-in users see them while managing their money; one message is for visitors asking the assistant on the public website. Default category names and the Want, Need and Must spending-priority tags are copied once into each newly registered user's data as their own editable names. "and {{count}} more" ends a list of AI model names inside another error.
/packages/frontend/src/i18n/locales/chun: These strings form the permission screen a user reaches when an AI assistant such as Claude or ChatGPT, added via Settings → AI → Connectors (MCP), redirects them to MoneyMatter to authorize access. Any user connecting such an app sees it, after signing in if needed, and approves or denies the app's request to view, change or delete their financial data. Each permission is a short label plus a description; "Optional" and "Always granted" are short badges on a permission, and "An application" stands in for the app name in the title when it is unknown.

These strings form the Forgot your password? and Set a new password screens, used by signed-out visitors (or anyone who opens a reset link from an email) to recover access to an account with email and password. The first screen asks for the account email, then shows a neutral "Check your email" message that does not reveal whether the account exists, with a resend link locked for a short seconds countdown; on instances without email delivery it says the reset is unavailable and to contact the administrator. The second screen is reached from the emailed link: the user enters and confirms a new password, or sees "Link invalid or expired" with a way to request a new link.

These strings form the Log in to account screen, where a person signs into an existing account with email and password, a passkey, or Google or GitHub, with a link to sign up instead. Only signed-out visitors see it, including people sent here to sign in before approving an AI assistant's access. The errors are login failures shown on the form or as a notification, and the tooltip about disabled signups appears only when the operator of this instance has closed registration. "Or continue with email" divides the provider buttons from the email form.

These strings form the Create an account screen, where a new visitor registers with email, display name and password, or with Google or GitHub, with a link back to sign in. Only signed-out visitors see it; the sign-ups-disabled error appears only when the operator of this instance has closed registration. "Verify Password" is the field for retyping the password, and the display-name field shows an example name as a hint. The passkey button labels here are shared with the Log in screen and do not appear on this one.

These strings form the Check your email screen shown right after someone registers with email and password, asking them to open the verification link sent to their inbox before they can sign in. Only a signed-out visitor who has just signed up sees it, and can resend the email (then locked for a short seconds countdown) or go back to sign in. The description is three pieces read as one text around the user's email address, the last starting with the period that ends the first sentence; the "Didn't receive the email?" line likewise ends in "or" and continues into the resend link.

These strings cover the Select Base Currency step a signed-in user must complete before first entering the app, and the brief "Completing sign in..." screen shown when returning from Google, GitHub or an email verification link. Base currency is the user's main currency, used to convert transactions in other currencies; on the hosted cloud service, users on the free trial also see how many days it lasts, with a link to plans. The sign-in error messages come in variants for signing in, signing up, and linking a Google or GitHub login from Settings → Security → Login Methods.

These strings appear across nearly every screen: shared buttons and labels, account types, payment methods, currency names, the date range picker, file uploads, notifications, and overlays shown while balances are recalculated. Signed-in users see most of them; sign-in and sign-up pages reuse a few, demo strings target people trying the public demo, and billing strings appear only on the hosted cloud service. Many are badges or fragments inserted into sentences (date filter words like before or between, "See plans" links inside banners), and "Session" in the import badge means an uploaded file held on the server, not a sign-in.

These strings appear in dialogs and confirmations that open over many screens across the app: editing transactions (splits, refunds, transfers, attachments, location, templates), attaching an invoice with AI, recording loan and recurring payments, managing portfolios, holdings, categories, account groups and currencies, and sharing accounts or budgets. Every signed-in user sees them while changing their data, including when accepting or declining a sharing invitation. Balance is money in an account or portfolio cash, and for a loan the amount still owed; Split means dividing one transaction across categories.

These strings appear across many screens rather than on one: generic error notifications for when a request to the server fails, the session expires, an import sends too much data at once or something unexpected goes wrong, plus the page-not-found screen. The long cannot-reach-the-server message appears only on self-hosted instances, whose users run the server themselves, and names a setting that must stay unchanged; the hosted cloud service shows the short one. The page-not-found screen is shown to anyone, signed in or not, who opens an address that matches no page.

These strings are labels, placeholders and validation messages for forms and pickers used across many screens: category, currency, account, tag, payee and budget selectors, plus forms for accounts, loans, vehicles, investment transactions, portfolio settings and portfolio cash deposits, withdrawals, transfers and currency exchanges. Signed-in users see them while entering data; the generic select strings also appear when a new user picks a base currency after sign-up. Make, Model and Trim describe a vehicle; mo abbreviates months after a number; lowercase transfer, deposit and withdrawal fill a confirmation sentence.

These strings belong to the app frame around every signed-in page: the main navigation with its account list, the Add transaction menu, bank sync and AI categorization status, the Quick Start checklist, the feedback dialog, and warnings about bank connections that need reconnecting. Every signed-in user sees them; users with no connected bank get a prompt to connect one, and users with no accounts see a welcome screen on the Dashboard. "Sync" means pulling data from a connected bank, "Connect" and "Reconnect" mean linking a bank rather than signing in, and Light, Dark and System are theme names.

These strings cover connecting a bank from the Accounts page: choosing a provider, its setup steps and help instructions, the screen shown after the bank's authorization, and a connection's page for syncing, reconnecting, renaming or disconnecting it. Every signed-in user can open it, but on the hosted cloud service bank connections depend on the user's plan, while self-hosted instances have them unlocked. Integration and connection mean the same bank link, Free and Paid say whether the third-party provider charges, and setup steps name buttons and fields on the provider's own website, not in MoneyMatter.

These strings are on an account's page, opened by selecting an account (for example on the Accounts page), with its Details, Data Connection, Sharing and Settings tabs, and on a vehicle's page, which tracks its estimated value, depreciation and manual value overrides. Owners see everything; people the account is shared with see their access level as a badge, and only owners and managers get the Sharing tab, which covers this one account. Balance is this account's balance, a system account is a manually updated one not linked to a bank, and on the vehicle page value replaces balance.

These strings are on the Accounts page, which lists a user's accounts grouped into Bank connections, Manual accounts, Shared with me, Vehicles and Archived, and lets them create an account, add a vehicle, connect a bank or open an account. Every signed-in user sees it; Shared with me holds accounts other users gave them access to. Total balance combines all accounts, Balance in the sort options orders by each account's balance, Active, Expiring soon and Expired are a bank connection's consent status, and Connect is a short form of Connect bank.

These strings are in the Analytics section of the main navigation: the Cash Flow, Trends Comparison, Pivot, Net Worth History, Net Worth Drivers, Contributions and Investment Projection reports plus their filters and chart settings. Every signed-in user sees it while studying income, spending, net worth and investments over time. Saved and Grown split net-worth change into money set aside versus market growth, while a saved view in Pivot is a stored report layout. Level {level} (category nesting depth) and Top {count} (number of largest categories shown) are short option labels.

These strings appear on the Transactions → Automations page, which lists the user's rules, and in the editor for creating or editing one. Signed-in users build rules that set a category, payee, tags or note on new transactions from bank sync or file imports, where the first matching rule wins, and can apply a rule to past transactions, which cannot be undone. Short fragments like "note has" or "merchant lacks" build a compact rule summary after "When" and "Then"; "Merchant" is the raw name from bank text, while "Payee" is the cleaned-up counterparty.

These strings appear on the page of a single budget, opened from the Planned → Budgets list, with Statistics, Transactions and Sharing tabs. Signed-in users review income, expenses and limit use by category and over time, and on manual budgets add or unlink transactions. Only the owner or a member with Manage access sees Sharing, where they invite people and set their access. "Net Balance" is the budget's income minus expenses, not an account balance; "Cancel" either leaves selection mode or withdraws a pending invitation.

These strings appear on the Planned → Budgets page, where users create, browse and archive budgets, and on a single budget's page opened from it, including its edit form and Add Transactions dialog. Signed-in users track spending over a date range against an optional limit, either with Category-based budgets that pick up transactions from chosen categories or with Manual budgets filled by hand. "Limit" is the spending cap, "Net" is the budget's income minus expenses, and "Shared by" marks a budget another person shared with the user.

These strings are on the Dashboard, the customizable home screen users land on after sign-in, built from widgets such as Balance Trend, Cash Flow, Net Worth, Latest Transactions, Subscriptions & Bills, Categories Watchlist, Credit Utilization and Planned, plus a Customize mode for adding and configuring them. Every signed-in user sees it for a quick overview of their finances. Saved in the Cash Flow widget is income minus expenses for the period, and Growth in the Net Worth widget is the total change in net worth, not market growth; pending planned transactions are scheduled entries that have not happened yet.

These strings are on the Settings → Household page, where a user runs their household: people they invite get access to every account they own, including ones added later. Any signed-in user can invite members, set their Read or Write access and remove them, and can leave other people's households they joined (Households I'm in). Write scope limits which transactions a member may edit; Pending marks an unaccepted invitation, whose Cancel and Resend act on that invitation; Remove drops a member, Leave drops the user from someone else's household.

These strings appear on the "Import from Wallet (BudgetBakers)" page, reached from Settings → Import/Export → Wallet (BudgetBakers), where the user uploads one or more CSV files exported from the Wallet app by BudgetBakers and moves through the Upload, Resolve, Review and Done steps. Any signed-in user moving their Wallet data into MoneyMatter uses it to link each Wallet account and category to an existing one or create a new one, then checks detected transfers and possible duplicates before importing. Out of wallet means a one-sided transfer to or from money outside the tracked accounts, not the Wallet app.

These strings are the CSV import wizard, reached from Settings → Import/Export → Import CSV, where the user uploads one or more bank CSV exports with the same columns, maps columns to transaction fields, links accounts, categories and tags to existing ones or creates them, checks duplicates and imports. Any signed-in user can use it to bring in their own transaction history. "Row" is a data row of the file, "unpriceable" rows use a currency with no stored exchange rate, and short strings like "transactions will be imported." follow a number.

These strings are on the Import History page, reached from Settings → Import/Export → Import History, which lists past runs of every import on that page (CSV, OFX or QFX, YNAB, Wallet (BudgetBakers), Microsoft Money and AI text-source imports) with their transaction and account counts, and opens the transactions each one created. Any signed-in user sees their own imports here, mainly to delete a whole import, optionally including a linked transfer transaction outside it. An import batch is everything one import run created, deleted together as one unit.

These strings appear on the "Import from Microsoft Money" page, reached from Settings → Import/Export → Microsoft Money, where the user uploads a .mny file from the discontinued Microsoft Money app and moves through the Upload, Map data, Review, Import and Done steps. Any signed-in user moving an old Money ledger into MoneyMatter uses it to link each Money account and category to an existing one or create a new one, then chooses whether to also import voided entries and possible duplicates. Out-of-wallet means a one-sided transfer to or from money outside the tracked accounts.

These strings are the OFX/QFX import wizard, reached from Settings → Import/Export → OFX or QFX statement, where the user uploads a bank or credit card statement file, maps its accounts, reviews duplicates and file warnings, and imports. Any signed-in user can use it to bring in transactions from their bank; the file warnings (missing or duplicate bank transaction IDs, fallback time zone) do not block the import. "Merged into planned" counts imported transactions matched to planned transactions the user entered ahead of time, not a subscription plan.

These strings are shared by the Import CSV, OFX or QFX statement, Import from YNAB, Wallet (BudgetBakers) and Microsoft Money wizards under Settings → Import/Export, not by the AI text-source import: linking source accounts and categories to existing ones or creating them, possible duplicates and balance changes. Signed-in users see them while mapping an import and picking duplicates to import anyway. "Target" is the existing account or category a source item links to, "Backfill rows" are older transactions that leave the current balance unchanged, and "CSV" in the duplicates table means the incoming row from any imported file.

These strings are the Statement Parser, reached from Settings → Import/Export → Import from any Text Source, where the user uploads bank statements (PDF, CSV or TXT), receipt photos or banking app screenshots (JPG, PNG or WebP), AI extracts their transactions, and the user picks or creates an account, reviews duplicates and imports them. Any signed-in user can use it; it runs on one of their own AI models if they added one, otherwise on MoneyMatter AI, the usage-limited model included in their plan, and large files can take minutes. "Tokens" and "Estimated Cost" refer to AI model usage, and "transactions", "from" and "in" are fragments placed around a count, bank name and currency.

These strings appear on the "Import from YNAB" page, reached from Settings → Import/Export → Import from YNAB, where the user uploads the Register.csv file from a YNAB budget export and moves through the Upload, Review and Done steps. Any signed-in user moving their YNAB data into MoneyMatter uses it to set the currency of each detected account or skip it, then reviews the accounts, categories, payees, tags, transactions and transfers to be created. Budget and Export budget in the upload hint are menu items inside YNAB, and Starting balance is a label for a YNAB account's opening balance.

These strings appear on the Import transactions page of one investment portfolio, opened from that portfolio's page, where the user uploads a broker or exchange file or pastes text to add buy, sell and dividend transactions; it is separate from the imports under Settings → Import/Export. Any signed-in user with a portfolio uses it: AI Import has AI extract the trades at an estimated token cost, CSV Import has the user map columns by hand, and both end in a review matching each ticker to a security (a tradable instrument). Side is the column giving each row's type; Currency in the review is the trade's settlement currency.

These strings appear on the Investments page (Accounts → Investments in the navigation), which lists the user's portfolios with actions to create, view or delete them, plus a Trash section of deleted portfolios. Every signed-in user sees it when managing their portfolios or restoring a deleted one. Trash keeps a deleted portfolio for a set number of days before erasing it, and "Delete now" erases it at once. "Hidden" marks a portfolio the user turned off, and {type} receives the portfolio type (Investment, Retirement, Savings or Other).

These strings appear on the Accounts → Loans page, which lists the user's mortgages, vehicle, student and other loans, and on the page of a single loan opened from it. Signed-in users add a loan with its principal, rate and term, record or link payments, archive or delete it, and project the payoff date under different monthly payments. "Balance" here is the debt still owed, not money in an account, "Balance as of" is the date that figure was fixed, and abbreviations like "mo", "yr" and "APR" sit in narrow table columns and chart labels.

These strings are on the Transactions → Optimizations page and the tools it opens: Transfer matching, which finds expense and income pairs to link as transfers between the user's own accounts, AI categorization, which lets AI pick categories for transactions still in the default category and keeps a history of runs, and a shortcut to apply an automation rule to past transactions. Every signed-in user can use it to clean up their transaction data. Model is the model in use, "AI model" the user's saved model providing it, and key that model's API key; Manual, Data import and Bank sync are short labels for what started a run.

These strings are on the Settings → Payees page, with its Manage and Settings tabs and each payee's detail page, and in the New Payee dialog, which can also open from payee pickers elsewhere, such as the transaction form. Every signed-in user sees them while cleaning up payees: renaming, merging, setting default categories, tags or locations for future transactions, and tuning automatic payee detection from bank data. A payee is the app's cleaned-up counterparty, while merchant name and aliases mean the raw text from the bank that gets matched to it; Net flow is income minus expenses for that payee.

These strings appear on the Planned → Recurring Payments page, the page of a single recurring payment and the Discover dialog that finds recurring payments in past transactions. Signed-in users track subscriptions, bills, installments and recurring income, set schedules and reminders, link bank transactions by rule, AI or by hand, and mark each due period paid or skipped. "Subscription" in running text usually means any recurring payment, "Cancel" closes a dialog rather than cancelling a subscription, and "Basics", "Schedule", "Automation" and "Organize" are sections of one payment's settings.

These strings appear on a single portfolio's page, opened from the Investments page, covering its value and returns, its holdings with each one's trades, and its cash per currency. Every signed-in user sees it while tracking one portfolio's securities and cash. In the Type column, "Cancel", "Transfer" and "Tax" are investment transaction types, not buttons, and the "Cash" column is the money actually paid or received for a trade. Many strings are narrow table headers ("AC/Share", "Cash ccy", "FX rate"), and "shares" follows a number.

These strings are on the Settings → Shared with me page, which lists the accounts, households and budgets other MoneyMatter users have shared with the signed-in user, plus pending invitations to review. It is the recipient's side of sharing: each entry shows who shared it and lets the viewer leave, giving up their access. Read, Write and Manage are short labels for the access level the viewer was given, and Untitled stands in for a shared item that has no name.

These strings are on the Transactions page, with its filters, bulk edit and delete, transaction groups and the Upcoming list of planned payments, and in the same transaction list, table and filters reused on the Dashboard, account, loan, portfolio and budget pages, Analytics and transaction-picking dialogs. Every signed-in user sees them while reviewing and editing their transactions. Planned means a scheduled entry that hasn't happened yet, and Confirm or Mark paid records that it did; Pending means the bank hasn't booked it yet. Many strings are narrow column headers, badges or filter labels.

These strings cover the Venture section (Accounts → Venture in the navigation): the list of the user's private venture deals (SPVs, syndicates, fund stakes), the "Manage platforms" page, and each deal's terms, metrics and events timeline. Every signed-in user sees it when tracking illiquid investments made outside a brokerage. A "platform" is the syndicate or fund manager (GP) invested through, not software, and "Outstanding" is a deal status meaning still held. TVPI, DPI, IRR, "P&L" and "Mgmt fee" are compact metric and fee labels.

These strings are on the Settings → Accounts groups page, where the user creates, renames and deletes groups that organize their accounts list, possibly nested in a parent group, and removes accounts from a group (accounts are added from each account's own page). Every signed-in user sees this page. Some groups were created by a bank connection; renaming, emptying or deleting them never affects the connection or its syncing, and "Connection" is a short badge for such a group. "in {name}" is a fragment naming the parent group, shown after an account count.

These strings appear on the Settings → Admin page, which is listed only for instance admins, the people who run this MoneyMatter server. Admins come here to trigger a price sync for all securities that users hold, or to upload historical security prices from a CSV or JSON file in a step-by-step dialog: pick a security, map file fields and the date format, preview differences from existing prices, set options and upload. A security here is a tradable investment such as a stock or fund, and a record is one dated price, not a transaction.

These strings appear in the Connectors (MCP) tab of the Settings → AI page. Signed-in users come here to connect an AI assistant such as Claude or ChatGPT to their MoneyMatter data through the MCP server URL, follow the setup steps for each assistant, and review or revoke active connectors. Button and field names inserted into the setup steps (Add custom connector, Add connector, Add, Connectors, Remote MCP server URL) are labels in Claude's and ChatGPT's own settings, not in MoneyMatter; scopes such as Read financial data and Offline access are permissions a connected assistant holds.

These strings appear on the Settings → AI page, in its AI Features and AI models tabs. In AI Features, signed-in users pick for each feature, such as transaction categorization and statement parsing, one of their own AI models or MoneyMatter AI, the model included in their plan, and write custom categorization instructions. In AI models they save models, each a provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google or a custom OpenAI-compatible server such as Ollama), a model name and an API key. The "Your key" badge means a feature runs on the user's own model and "Server" on MoneyMatter AI; both also show on the AI text-source import screen.

These strings are on the Settings → Appearance page, where a signed-in user sets personal display preferences: the theme (light, dark or following the device), which sections appear in the app's sidebar, and whether amounts show short currency symbols instead of ISO codes. Every signed-in user sees this page, except the Header section with its "Support button" toggle, which appears only on self-hosted instances. A symbol here is a currency sign such as $ or ₴, and "Header" and "Sidebar" name parts of the app's own navigation.

These strings are on the Settings → Categories page, where the user creates, edits and deletes the categories and subcategories that classify their transactions and moves a category under a different parent or to the top level. Every signed-in user sees this page. In "Organize" mode the user drags categories to queue several moves and saves them together; "Top level" means a category with no parent, and the short drag-and-drop errors explain why a drop target is not allowed.

These strings are on the Settings → Currencies page, where the user adds the currencies they hold money in, sets each one's exchange rate (live market rate or a custom one), deletes currencies no account uses, and changes the base currency that all balances, totals and reports convert into. Every signed-in user sees this page; changing the base currency is a rare, heavy step that recalculates every transaction's reference amount and is blocked while the user is in a household or shares an account with someone. "Base", "Live", "Custom" and "Unused" are short status labels on a currency.

These strings appear on the Settings → Import/Export page, in its Import and Export tabs; the back link and import source names also show on each import screen and in Import History. Signed-in users come here to pick an import source (CSV file, OFX or QFX statement, YNAB, Wallet (BudgetBakers), Microsoft Money, or any text read by AI) or to download their data as a zip in JSON, CSV or Excel format, choosing a date range, accounts and which data sets to include. YNAB, Wallet (BudgetBakers) and Microsoft Money are names of other finance apps.

These strings are on the Settings → General page, where the user chooses how their financial data is calculated and entered: credit limits in balances, transfer matching with manual accounts, pending bank transactions, savings categories, the Quick Start guide, account-picker defaults, upcoming scheduled payments in the transactions list, and optional transaction-form fields including a location map picker. Every signed-in user sees this page. "Balance" here is an account balance, never a budget remainder, and "pending" means a bank transaction the bank has not booked yet.

These strings label the Settings menu: one item per settings page (Appearance, Language, Security, Currencies, Categories, Tags, Payees, Scheduled payments, Household and more), two group headings, and the "Back to Settings" link that returns to the menu. Every signed-in user sees them; "Admin" appears only for instance admins, and "Plan & billing" only on the hosted cloud service, never on self-hosted instances or demo accounts. The heading "Personal" groups the user's own preferences and login security, and "Workspace" groups the setup of their financial data.

These strings are on the Settings → Language page, where a signed-in user picks the language of the app interface; the list includes community languages translated by volunteers on Crowdin, in which untranslated text falls back to English. Every signed-in user sees this page, and the choice changes only their own interface. A closing section invites the user to fix or add translations or request a new language on Crowdin, or on the public feature board instead; "feature board" is link text inserted into the sentence around it.

These strings appear on the Settings → Plan & billing page, which exists only on the hosted cloud service and is hidden on self-hosted instances and for demo accounts. Signed-in users come here to check their trial or subscription status, subscribe to or switch between the Essential and Plus plans and monthly or yearly billing, manage payment in the Stripe billing portal, and vote for the planned Premium plan. Essential, Plus, Premium and Early Adopter are plan names, and a household seat is one person the user can share data with; prices, dates and trial-day counts must stay exact.

These strings appear on the Settings → Security page, in its Login Methods, Active Sessions, Password, Backup & restore and Danger Zone tabs; restore progress messages can also cover any screen while a restore runs. Signed-in users manage sign-in methods (password, OAuth accounts, passkeys) and devices, change their password, back up or restore their data, wipe it, or delete their account. A backup is a zip of all the user's data, not a spare sign-in method; "account" is the MoneyMatter login in Delete your account but a financial account in the data lists, and "securities" are investment instruments.

These strings are on the Settings → Scheduled payments page, which holds one preference for the recurring payments tracked under Planned → Recurring Payments: whether new ones start with auto-record switched on, meaning the app itself records the payment as a transaction on its due date. Every signed-in user sees this page; it only sets the default, and each recurring payment can still change it. "Subscription" in these strings means any recurring payment the user creates, not their MoneyMatter plan.

These strings are on the Settings → Tags page, where the user creates, edits and deletes tags (name, color, icon, optional description) that label transactions, and sets up reminders on a tag. Every signed-in user sees this page. A reminder either warns when spending with that tag exceeds an amount or reports that tagged transactions exist, triggered as soon as a transaction is tagged or checked daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly or yearly; "Enabled" and "Disabled" are a reminder's status, and the icon search strings are also reused when picking a category icon.
